notes.title: DEVLOG #23 - Project Regolith's Postmortem, What Comes Next?
notes.content:
Hey there everyone, we're back from our short rest this week, and I wanted to start the week with a pretty important update. Today I'm gonna be going over some of our key talking points following a post-mortem discussion the team had before we took our break this past week, and then covering what's next for us as a studio.

This process marked the official conclusion of our major support patches for the game post-launch, and we're now much happier with the state of the game, performance and bug-wise, but we still have plenty to talk about concerning the game, it's dev cycle, and a slew of other things across the board.

[h1]Project Regolith's Postmortem[/h1]
A week ago, just after launching patch 1.04 for Project Regolith, we sat down as a team and had a thorough discussion about the last 20 months of development. We thought it would be a good idea to share the major talking points with you all as a way to provide a bit of closure to the project as a whole. So, let's start with a bit of an overview before getting into specifics.

[h2]Project Overview[/h2]
Ever since the end of March of 2022, we've been working on Project Regolith, and on the last day of October of 2023 we released the full game to the public - Our first commercial game after 3 years of study, and 1 year of business development. Originally, we had a few major goals: one was to build a short co-op experience inspired by the likes of [url=https://store.steampowered.com/app/582500/We_Were_Here/]We Were Here[/url], [url=https://store.steampowered.com/app/1335790/Operation_Tango/]Operation: Tango[/url], [url=https://store.steampowered.com/app/1435790/Escape_Simulator/]Escape Simulator[/url], and a whole lot more that I'll refrain from naming in the interest of saving a bit of writing time.

Another was to build the foundation of our studio, establish reliable workflows, and begin to make a name for ourselves in the Australian Game Dev scene. And lastly, of course, to prove our ability to work to a timeline and help make a case for more official funding/publishing channels for future projects (more on that later!).

The past 20 months have been an incredible learning experience for all of us on the team, from building new working relationships with voice artists, improving our technical skills, developing marketing materials, working events, and so, SO much more. We feel as though we've at least partially hit the mark on each of our outlined goals.

All-in-all, we're proud of the work we've done on Project Regolith, although the game hasn't pushed as far as we'd hoped in terms of sales, we're still extremely happy with the development of both our skills and our working pipelines over the course of the project. However, we'd be remiss not to address the state of the game on launch, and the steps we've taken this past month to rectify it.

[h2]Launch Issues[/h2]
At the very end of October, Project Regolith went live, and right away players spotted issues we'd missed, some fairly critical, and some that were more minor that we had leeway to fix. As well as a handful of issues we [i]were[/i] aware of, but had run out of time to fix. This unfortunately meant that the game, despite being technically feature, and story complete, still felt unfinished and very rough.

[i][b]So, why did this happen?[/b][/i]
Throughout the course of development, getting people on-board to help test the game was always on our minds. However, in a lot of cases we were apprehensive to organize these kinds of testing sessions due to features still being incomplete, puzzles missing vital context clues or components, networking issues, among other reasons.

At the end of the day, we were being very precious about our testing process. A mindset that definitely cost us dearly when we finally clicked the big green "Release" button.

[i][b]How do we remedy this process in the future?[/b][/i]
Well, a recurring theme I'll be touching on throughout this entire write-up is [i][b]EXPERIENCE[/b][/i]. In our previous works as students, games we'd worked on were often much, MUCH smaller in scope. This meant less features, far fewer moving parts, and a more easily-defined testing process.

Knowing what we know now about larger projects like ProjReg, and how easily things can fall apart without a proper testing framework, we'll be able to focus on a more rigid, well-organized pipeline for testing new features, scoping out more time for keeping all these moving parts in order, and generally avoiding these kinds of issues in the future.

Speaking of timelines and scope, this transitions well into what I'd like to surmise next...

[h2]Timeline Management[/h2]
When we'd outlined our intentions for Scope back in October of 2022, when we launched our Kickstarter campaign for voice acting, we'd originally cited a release window of Early Q3 of this year. Some roadblocks we'd encountered regarding funding (which I'll be covering next), and some big marketing opportunities for the studio that we couldn't pass up in the form of PAX Aus and SXSW Sydney ended up pushing us back slightly. In the end, we still managed to hit our new deadline of late October (in spite of some awkward build approval issues too, whoops).

All up, we're pleased with our timeline management, and also happy with our decision making earlier in the year when it came to the original delays, and our transparency in announcing them. This is something we're hoping to maintain going forward.

A major influence on these timelines, however, comes in the form of...

[h2]Funding[/h2]
As long-term followers of the project may know, back in January of 2023 we'd approached a couple of Government bodies here in Australia with pitches to secure some additional funding for Project Regolith's development, which were ultimately unsuccessful after a lengthy review and reapplication process. This was the major roadblock that contributed to our initial delay I mentioned earlier. The general consensus was that due to our inexperience, and lack of any backlog of titles, we weren't a safe bet for investment, which is a reasonable conclusion.

While we were disheartened, we were still committed to finishing Project Regolith, come hell or high water. Thanks to the Academy of Interactive Entertainment's Incubator Program, we still had a small fund to draw from for major marketing events and materials, plus the generous contributions from our Kickstarter backers for voice talent. All other costs on the project were covered out of pocket by those of us on the dev team.

With most of the team working full-time on this, and part-time on other commitments and jobs, funding is still a bit of a sore spot for us. It's our hope that with Project Regolith under our belt as a released title, we'll be more seriously considered by publishers and/or funding bodies next time.

With the more external influences out of the way, let's reflect more about the actual gameplay elements of ProjReg...

[h2]Puzzles and World Design (Warning: Spoilers Ahead!)[/h2]
When we'd first set out to build Project Regolith, we'd had a handful of ideas for cooperatively-charged puzzles, and a vision of some fanciful non-Euclidean mechanics to help spice them up. In most cases, particularly the front half of the game, we feel we achieved our initial vision. While [spoiler]Life Support[/spoiler], the first "official" puzzle the players encounter features no non-Euclidean elements, the steady ramp up of these elements from [spoiler]Refinery through to Hydroponics[/spoiler] feels pretty good to us.

We're particularly proud of those first four major sections - [spoiler]Life Support, Refinery, Quarantine, and Hydroponics[/spoiler] are definitely the highlights of the game's puzzle designs, which is unfortunate, because it meant that the back half was lacking.

To get specific, [spoiler]the Terraforming Lab, and Admin Department[/spoiler] puzzles are definitely not as well-explained to players, and have a more abstract feel to them. This was due to a mixture of design burnout, some over-scoping, and networking limitations that forced some changes in our original design plans.

Looking ahead, we're planning on how we can best take advantage of our strengths and ideas to build something that's more engaging all throughout the game.

[h2]Narrative[/h2]
Thanks to our Kickstarter backers, we were able to deliver a fully-voiced narrative to Project Regolith in the form of the game's audio logs. We're extremely grateful to have been able to work with such an amazingly talented cast to pull off what we have.

That said, the casting process (which we had originally documented in devlogs #8 through #10) took a massive toll on both myself and Ryan, and definitely took a lot more time than we'd originally expected, although I suppose 360 applicants to review will do that.

Another important narrative-related issue that we became more aware of as we went was our pacing. Many of our audio logs run for 60+ seconds, which creates either a lot of downtime, or moments where players are waiting for one audio log to finish before interacting with the next. This saturation was in part due to us overestimating how many additional side logs we'd need to have written to accommodate all our "Name an NPC" Backers, whilst also being able to give attention to our main cast, and the main story of Outpost Rhea. Essentially, we had too much story with not enough time to tell it.

The audio-log format of the game also meant that integrating narrative into what was actively happening to the players in-the-moment was a little more difficult than expected, and it led to the major narrative beats feeling a little disjointed and confusing to some.

We'll make sure we avoid similar mistakes in the future with a more refined narrative-writing process, making a more consistent plan for story beats and making sure the team is clear on how each of them can be integrated with the game at appropriate times.

[h2]Mechanics and Systems[/h2]
At last, we come to my wheelhouse. As the game's sole programmer/technical lead, I have a lot of gripes about how I'd handled systems built in the early phases of development coming back to haunt me as we got into the more complicated sections of the game.

This was not only my first commercial title, but also my first as an actual programmer, as I'd originally studied Design instead. Some might say making a networked multiplayer game as your first game is a bad idea.

To that, I'd say, [i]"Yes. Yes it was."[/i]

But the experience has been well worth it. The main takeaways I've taken from this project revolve around the importance of being consistent as a programmer, making sure everything is well-documented, and built with future systems in mind. Overall, I'm incredibly proud of my contributions to the game, and I'm super excited to keep working with the rest of the guys!

[h2]Art and Visuals[/h2]
A lot of our internal discussion about our Art pipeline has related to just generally being a bit more organized. Virtually everyone that's put their hands on ProjReg has been impressed with it's visuals, and even more impressed when told that it was all done by one person!

If there's one major point we'd want to focus on for future works in the art department, it would be speeding up our SetDressing and Lighting pipelines using a whole bunch of better practices we've picked up throughout this project.

[h2]Marketing[/h2]
When it comes to marketing for Project Regolith, personally I'm of two minds - Our in-person efforts/events felt really successful. We got to meet literally hundreds of people, expand our professional networks massively, and get a measurable increase in our analytics for wishlists, demo plays, etc. But, our digital efforts were almost the opposite, for a couple of reasons:

1. Social Media is HARD. It's not really a secret, but getting likes, follows, and general engagement isn't easy. Especially without a dedicated marketing person/team.

And 2. Splitting our time up when everyone on the team is already wearing 2-4 different hats made it difficult to find the spare time to schedule posts, edit trailers and TikToks, and generally market the game (and ourselves to an extent) digitally.

Over the past few weeks, I've seen a lot of great marketing talks, and spoken to some really wonderful people about how we can improve, and there's really no easy answer for this other than to make the time we have count. Starting next project, all of us will be putting in more effort to the marketing department!

[h2]Conclusion[/h2]
So, this has easily been our longest devlog yet, and likely the final devlog under the banner of "Project Regolith". What can we take away from all of this?

Well, 20 months ago we were fresh out of our studies, learning how to run a business and making a game at the same time. Here we are today, that game is done, for better or worse, and it's time to look towards the future.

There was a lot to look back on with Project Regolith. A lot of good, a lot of bad, but thankfully not a lot of ugly. Most of the processes and practices we've built are a fantastic foundation to keep building from, and most importantly...

We're richer for this experience, we know we have what it takes to not only make something, but to throw it out into the world. A lot of people have told us that just getting to this point is an achievement in itself, and that we should be proud to have made it this far. And we are proud, but, we're going to go further.

[h1]So, what comes next for Regolith Interactive?[/h1]
The four of us are really excited to say that we're starting on something new very soon. In fact, we've already started the pre-production process!

While we're not ready to share a whole lot of details right now, we hope you'll stick around for the ride. Check in with us on our socials and in our Discord where we'll be keeping everyone up-to-date on any important news from the studio.

notes.title: 9th of November, 2023 - Patch 1.02
notes.content:
Hi there everyone, today we're publishing the 2nd patch for Project Regolith, addressing a number of missing colliders, some issues with world-space portals, a missing achievement trigger, and some other things! Check out our full patch notes below:

[u][b]Project Regolith Update, 9th of November, 2023 - Patch 1.02[/b][/u]
- Fixed a massive performance issue being caused by a check that should've only been run once on the Main Menu. Framerates should be a little more stable on all machines now.

- Made some adjustments to the player's cameras to (hopefully) reduce noticeable clipping through world-space portals.

- Fixed an issue that was preventing an achievement related to [spoiler]the Atrium doors opening, revealing Cronus X[/spoiler] from firing.

- Restored a missing label from the players' settings menus for Caption Opacity. This was previously labelled correctly on the main menu but not during gameplay.

- Fixed an issue that was causing some specific Puzzle-related objects, such as the [spoiler]"Unstable" Model Car in the Admin Puzzle[/spoiler] being respawned in the wrong place when using the "Respawn Objects" pause menu button.

- Updated a few interaction prompts that were displaying the default placeholder "Interact With This Thing" text to display the correct prompt instead.

- Updated some of the prompts on the [spoiler]Terraforming Puzzle's interactable terminals[/spoiler] to better reflect some components that can be interacted with.

- Fixed a number of missing collision issues.

- Fixed some world-space portals being culled/not rendering at incorrect times.

- Fixed the Key Rebinding Settings tab in the Main Menu not displaying the unchangeable bindings for "Display Directive", "Open Codex", and "Text Chat".

- Fixed the End Credits UI being displayed smaller than intended.

- Fixed a missing sound cue on the [spoiler]Atrium Viewing Shutter[/spoiler], more door-related missing SFX fixes will be coming with next week's patch!

----------------------------------------------------------------------

That's all for this week - We're aiming to have another patch next week addressing some more noticeable world-space portal culling, as well as some general level culling/pop-in and out issues with the map.

Thanks for your patience,
- Conor and the Regolith Team

notes.title: An Important Update Regarding Launch
notes.content:
[h3]Hey everyone, we'd like to share an update regarding the planned launch of Project Regolith.[/h3]

These past few weeks we've been promoting that Project Regolith would be launching this Friday, the 27th of October. We've been committed to this date for the past couple of months, but unfortunately, there's been a series of hiccups in Steam's build review process, and it's looking like we're not going to be approved for release by Valve's team in time to hit our deadline.

To be fully transparent about the issue:
Early this morning we were notified that the Steam Review Team has been having connectivity issues that we hadn't yet encountered in our testing and review build of the game that we were planning to set live tomorrow. After a lot of experimentation today we're fairly confident we've ID'd the problem and implemented a fix, BUT this fix still needs to go through Steam's review process again, which can take a few days depending on their queue density.


[h3]So, what does this mean for launch?[/h3]

Unless we get a miraculous reply from the Steam team early tomorrow morning during their office hours declaring that they're no longer having the connection problem, [b]it seems we'll be pushing back launch by a few days at the very least.[/b]

We're fully aware of how frustrating this may be for those of you who've been keen to get your hands on the game, and trust me when I say that nobody's more frustrated at the situation than us.

Admittedly, blame for this issue lies on us as a team for leaving this review process so late, and not accounting for potential tech issues on Steam's end.

I know this sucks to hear, and it definitely sucks to write - So we'd like to apologize to you all for the delay. The moment we have more info we'll be sharing it via our [url=https://discord.gg/EpwKaVbJfk]Discord[/url].

- The Regolith Team

notes.title: Public Devlog #17 - The Prestige
notes.content:
[h3]Hi everyone, welcome to this weeks Devlog.[/h3]
This week we'd like to try something a little different, and talk about some of the technical details behind one of our more important non-Euclidean mechanics. To show you how the sausage is made, i'm gonna hand this update over to Regolith's lead programmer Conor Calam.

[h2]How its made: World Portals[/h2]

Hi I'm Conor, the lead programmer and technical designer behind Project Regolith. Today i'm going to demonstrate the inner workings of a mechanic we've internally dubbed "World Portals".

To give a quick demonstration of what I mean, here's an example that you see in our Trailer from a few weeks ago: 

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/43307026/61aa39d789c1224ddf901cd0033e2e5eb0fedf64.gif[/img]

World Portals serve a handful of functions in the game - In some cases as part of puzzles, and in others just as a fun little nod to the events behind Outpost Rhea's destabilization, and in others still as a way for us as developers to play with your heads a little.

Another example that everyone may be familiar with by now is the reflected ceiling from our Hydroponics Demo, and it serves as a better point for how World Portals can play into gameplay beyond a single visual trick: 

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/43307026/f71c2a11f1e50c006e60275082c3594ad82664b4.png[/img]

[i]"But how do they work?"[/i] I hear you ask. [i][b]The short answer[/b][/i] is: Unity's Render Texture system, a custom screen-space shader, some calculations made in code, and an extra render pass all working in tandem to help build the illusion of a continuous space.

[b][i]The long answer[/i][/b] gets a little more complicated. And to start explaining it, I'll have to pull back the curtain a little more. Here's what the Hydroponics ceiling looks like [b]BEFORE[/b] any of our lighting, post-processing, or Portal rendering is applied to it: 

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/43307026/a9f5cb6b57f9b7a66038c0ef606936a485e3f0eb.png[/img]

It all begins with a blank plane. The first step is linking this plane to it's twin at the opposite player's room, then calculating the position of our portal rendering camera relative to the player's position compared to the plane.

After that, a snapshot of what that "fake" camera can see is run through a custom screen-space shader, which adjusts what the camera "sees" to better line up with the environment that the portal is linked to.

Lastly, the "fake" camera's projection is sent to a Render Texture, where it is then applied to the plane, resulting in the illusion that we see in-game! 

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/43307026/b6b4b3ea1f5c3a2e07e143f956c219e178bb8447.png[/img]


[h3]Thanks to Conor for that explanation [/h3]
We hope this has been an interesting look into one of our most prominent non-Euclidean mechanics and/or you enjoyed a look into the world of game development. Let us know what you think of this style of post for future updates! In a couple of weeks time we'll be back to our regularly scheduled programming, where we talk about our final approach to PAX, Steam Next-Fest, and SXSW Sydney...

But until then, take care of yourselves!

-Ryan

notes.title: Public Devlog #13: Gold Milestone and Launch Window
notes.content:
[h3]Hello once again everyone, and welcome to this very special development update![/h3]

[url=https://store.steampowered.com/news/app/2220420/view/3671044735536723893]Last update we outlined how the project had shaped up during Beta.[/url] This week we'll be talking about our final Milestone coming up in the next few months, the Gold Milestone. We'd also like to spend a bit of time talking about our plans for Marketing, and the final launch window for Project Regolith. So without further ado, let's get right down to it...

[h2]The Gold Milestone[/h2]
As our final production milestone leading up to launch, our approach to Gold can be summed up broadly by the phrase "Get the game finished", but of course, there's a lot of work that's going to go into it, so let's talk details:

[b]Puzzles and Environments[/b] - It should come as no surprise that making sure all our environments are up-to-scratch in our main puzzle areas is a top priority for the team. While we mentioned last update that all our puzzles are in a playable state in a vacuum, there's still a ways to go in terms of environmental storytelling and environmental cues that help provide context or hints to certain puzzles narrative-wise. And that will be a major part of our focus throughout Gold.

[b]Narrative[/b] - Somewhat tying in to environmental work is our Narrative elements. As we've made a point of discussing in our updates, we've got a whole slew of Voice Actors whose work we've been receiving, reviewing, and preparing to implement into the game. The crew members of Outpost Rhea have their voices, and making sure they're heard in the right place and at the right time is something we're talking about. You'll also be able to revisit logs you've previously found, review transcripts, and read additional lore entries in our in-game Codex!

[b]Polish and Testing[/b] - I mentioned in our last update that external testing wasn't something we'd had much time for during Beta, and we're definitely aiming to remedy that as we push through the next few months. We're currently planning out when, where, and how we intend to get the game tested, and we'll hopefully talk a bit more about it in a future post.

Once we've got some solid, actionable data from our testers, we'll get to work on sanding down rough edges, fixing as many bugs as we can leading to launch, and overall making the game experience better!


[h2]Marketing[/h2]
As you might've guessed, marketing an Indie title is no small feat. We've been steadily growing our following on social media the past few months, but not at a pace we're particularly pleased with. Unfortunately, being a small team of 4 limits the amount of time we can spend engaging on Socials without taking time away from the actual production. We've been looking into other means of promotion for Project Regolith, and we've come up with a few ideas:

[b]Social Media Goals/Calls to Action[/b] - To try help drive engagement on our socials we've started setting incremental goals for each avenue. The first of which has been our effort to hit 200 Followers on our Twitter with a payoff of unlocking the 2nd Track from our OST (speaking of which, don't forget to check out the teaser below and subscribe to our YouTube!)

[previewyoutube=dlAHag757z0;full][/previewyoutube]

[b]Upcoming Events[/b] - Some of you may remember seeing us at PAX Australia 2022 last year, and showcasing our progress again this year is definitely something we want to leave on the table. Not only that, but we've also been considering South By Southwest Sydney (SXSW) as a candidate for promoting Project Regolith here in Australia. While nothing's set in stone just yet, we'll be sure to keep you all posted on events we'll be attending!

[b]The Steam Next-Fest (October 2023 Edition)[/b] - If you've been on Steam the past couple of weeks you no doubt noticed the June edition of the Steam Next-Fest, a showcase of upcoming Indie titles, livestreams, and playable Demos. This October the Next-Fest is returning once again, and we're intending to participate with Project Regolith, and a refurbished/relaunched version of our Hydroponics demo, with all of it's final assets in place.

Unfortunately, this has fairly important implications on our launch window, as titles that participate in the Next-Fest [b]can't[/b] be already released.


[h2]Launch Window[/h2]
So what does this mean for launch? Well, ultimately we're aiming to keep our deadlines the same, with the game being done by late-August, and leaving us with some wiggle-room for all the things we've outlined above. But in order to participate, we'll have to push back our planned launch-window by a little bit.

After a lengthy discussion amongst the team, we've decided that it would be silly to pass up an opportunity to help push the game to as many eyes as possible leading up to launch, and we've decided that this small delay is necessary. (It also moves us away from the launch windows of some much larger AAA Sci-Fi titles in late August/early September)

For this delay, we'd like to apologize. We hope you all understand the reasoning behind our decision. But we'd like to officially declare...

[h3][b][u]Project Regolith will release this October, following the conclusion of the Steam Next-Fest![/u][/b][/h3]

We'll leave you with that exciting bit of news for this week's update. Stay tuned for more information over the next few weeks! 

- Ryan

notes.content:
[h3]Hello, and welcome to our final steam update for the Beta milestone![/h3]

In case you missed it, [url=https://store.steampowered.com/news/app/2220420/view/3666539867375104525?l=english]a couple of weeks [/url]ago we talked a bit about the sounds behind Outpost Rhea, showed off 'The Hydroponics Lab' track from the game's OST, and teased a new track, '"Routine" Maintenance' to be released once we reach 200 Twitter followers:

[previewyoutube=dlAHag757z0;full][/previewyoutube]
Be sure to follow us on [url=https://twitter.com/Regolith_Int]Twitter[/url], if you haven't already, if you wanna hear the full track.

[h2]Beta Progress[/h2]
The past couple of months of updates have been heavily focused on SFX, Music, and Voice Acting. With Gold milestone fast approaching, we figured it's long overdue to talk again about progress on the actual game. Back in early April, we discussed our Journey Into Beta, and outlined a series of goals:

[list]
[*] [b]Major Puzzles[/b] connected by spaces that are sufficiently detailed and make reasonable in-universe sense to be there. 
[*] [b]Critical bugs are minimized[/b] to reduce programming workload leading to launch. 
[*][b] VA Casting completed for all Major and Minor roles[/b], with Major roles recorded and pending any required script changes/re-recordings. 
[*] [b]Player and Puzzle-specific SFX recorded[/b], most ambient and other non-priority sounds pending. 
[*] [b]Testing data on puzzle difficulty and readability[/b] ready to inform possible changes. 
[/list]
With our internal deadline for Beta coming up, now seems like a perfect time to talk about these goals, and how the team feels we're progressing towards them.

[h3]Music, SFX, and VA Casting and Recording [/h3]
We've spoken at length about our sounds the past few updates, so to keep it brief here - We're pretty happy with our progress on this front. - Not only is our entire VA Cast decided, we've also had the game's OST in the final stages of production with Simon, as well as a varied range of SFX coming in for specific puzzle and environmental elements aboard the station.

[h3]Puzzle Functionality [/h3]
As Beta has progressed the past few months, we've made a concentrated effort on puzzle functionality. As it stands today, each of our major puzzles is playable and solvable within a vacuum. You're probably asking "What does that actually mean?" though.

Let's say we were to drop you into one of our puzzles as it is right now, with ZERO context, ZERO clues, and ZERO guidance. Just you and a bunch of random puzzle elements. Given enough time, you'd probably be able to work out specifics and complete the puzzle, but it'd take a lot longer than what we'd like for the final product, and you probably wouldn't have too much fun with the guesswork.

At the end of the day, the puzzles are "solvable", but are missing a lot of quality-of-life and narrative features that'll make them launch-ready. As we continue to get our VA Audio implemented in-engine, the gap between now and Gold will steadily close.

[h3]Bug Fixes[/h3] 
As you might come to expect in any software field, bug fixing is a steady and ongoing task. But on the programming side, we're feeling pretty good about the state of things. Since our patch to the demo at the end of March this year we haven't encountered any serious issues with Networking, and despite the occasional small issue popping up in testing, things are looking and feeling good. Although, speaking of testing...

[h3]Testing Data[/h3]
We've been discussing how best to tackle a few elements of testing, particularly focused on "Fun" testing - Making sure the puzzles as they are right now are fun to play and solve. - Admittedly, we haven't had much opportunity to see the puzzles played by third-parties so far. Something we're aiming to remedy as we move towards Launch.

Originally we had planned to have some testing data before the end of Beta production, however, this hasn't really panned out as we'd hoped. For now, the goal posts have been moved back for testing into early Gold production, which will be running from July through to the end of August.

And lastly, you may have noticed I'd neglected to mention the first goal: Connecting the Major Puzzles together...


[h2]Environment Glow-ups[/h2]
A major part of our environmental workflow in Project Regolith is modular pieces. Not only because it makes building areas simpler, but it also makes sense that deep-space construction would be done using modular materials. One of our major concerns though, was that a lot of the station may end up looking too similar and areas we wanted to stand out more would blend together with others.

Our solution for this was to adjust the workflow slightly, and also split our pieces into a couple of categories - One that fits the more sterile and industrial elements of the station, such as the Engineering department or Maintenance areas - And another that feels a little more livable, suited for more "Civilian" aspects of the station.

In a couple of rarer cases, we've also got more purpose-built areas that don't fit this modular mold perfectly... But we'll save those for another update.

For now - Here's a peek at this workflow in action with some work-in-progress lighting with the Hydroponics puzzle found in the Steam Demo:

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/43307026/4fec0422a4d224b560b1a37b1f086fc6065437fd.gif[/img]

Ultimately, we're a lot happier with the cleaner style of the new area. We're excited to share some more progress shots of the space as the lighting is improved and we move closer to launch. And if you preferred the older look, not to worry, plenty of other areas will be maintaining that more industrial modular style!

And with that, today's update comes to a close and so does the Beta milestone! Next time we'll be talking a bit more about our goals lfor the Gold milestone, and what that'll mean for the project! 'Til then, you can get more updates and content on our socials!

notes.title: Public Devlog #9 - VA Update, The TC Corp, and Outpost Rhea
notes.content:
[h3]Hey there once again folks, welcome to this fortnight's devlog
[/h3]
If you're up to date with [url=https://steamcommunity.com/games/2220420/announcements/detail/3721705159484642501] our last post[/url], you'd know that we'll have wrapped up our VA Casting process! Today I'd like to give you all a short update on what's next for Casting, and go in-depth on the driving force behind the events of the game - The TerraCaelum Corporation - and their deep space magnum opous, Outpost Rhea, the location you'll find yourselves exploring throughout Project Regolith.


[h2]VA Update[/h2]
Over the past couple of weeks, Conor and I finished listening through, categorizing, and parring down our massive list of over 300 auditions, and subsequent 80-ish callbacks! We've been having preliminary meetings with our choices for main cast members, and we're planning to publish an official cast list once we've finished making sure everyone's on-board! look forward to that during the next devlog!


[h2]The TerraCaelum Corporation[/h2]
The TerraCaelum Corporation (or TCC for short) are at the forefront of Project Regolith's narrative, an Earth-based private company with their reach beginning to extend into the stars - TCC contracts a multitude of Earth's best corporate and scientific minds with the goal of extending Humanity's borders beyond Sol.

As Humans developed spacefaring technology and began to establish larger, more purpose-built space stations throughout our home in the Sol System, the executives at TCC began dreaming up plans for a deep-space research facility where their contractors could perform advanced studies and help further Human understanding of foreign worlds. This station was dubbed "Outpost Rhea", named for the Engineer who headed the planning and blueprinting of the Station's first iteration.


[h2]Outpost Rhea[/h2]
As decades passed, Outpost Rhea's operations have expanded significantly - with a fresh batch of staff arriving every couple of years in "Rotation Vessels", large autopiloted transport ships that make the 5-year-long trip to and from Rhea to deliver personnel in cryo-sleep. These new crew members pursue a multitude of ventures, answering to a select few superiors whom in turn report to the Director of Operations aboard Rhea, Gustavo Dos Reis Castro.

Recent years aboard Rhea have been eventful, following the discovery of a peculiar space-time anomaly that has seen most of the crew's efforts shift in focus on the orders of Director Castro, and Rhea's Chief Science Officer, Gary Langden, who see an opportunity to develop a new cutting-edge piece of technology.

Feeling a major breakthrough coming, Castro and Langden authorize a new experiment, one that is sure to cement their legacies and validate their time aboard Outpost Rhea. An experiment that would be dubbed [b]"Project Regolith"[/b]...


... Buuuuut that's all we're telling you guys for now! We'll see you all in a couple of weeks for our exciting cast reveal!

notes.title: Public Devlog #8 - The Bots, VA Casting Progress Update
notes.content:
[h2]Hello once again, and welcome to this week's community update!
[/h2]

The past couple weeks have been eventful for us here in the office - We've been hard at work categorizing, reviewing, and sending out callbacks for our VA Casting process as outlined in our post from [url=https://store.steampowered.com/news/app/2220420/view/7073508075346322566] a few weeks ago.[/url]

We've got an update on the VA process for you all, as well as a look at the two stars of Project Regolith, the player characters themselves - The Hermes-class LPM (Lightweight Planetary Mapper), and the Hephaestus-class HIL (Heavyweight Industrial Loader), although members of our[url=https://discord.gg/KkNxqHduxJ] Discord [/url] may know them better by their dev nicknames, LightBot and HeavyBot!


[h2]VA Casting Progress Update[/h2]
Initially when we outlined our goals for VA Casting, we had set a casting deadline for the 1st of May, what we hadn't accounted for was the sheer number of people we'd end up receiving interest from. Sitting at just over 300 audition reels, myself and Conor have been listening to, reviewing, and categorizing dozens upon dozens of actors each day - And while we've completed the Callback phase for the game's cast, we were a couple of days behind schedule for two of the roles that had the most auditions sent in.

In the long run, this shouldn't cause any major issues. Casting for a majority of roles will be done on-schedule, and the remainder will be done less than a week following that.

We've been incredibly impressed by a lot of the auditions we've heard so far, and we can't wait to share the names and work of our final cast in a few weeks time!


[h2]The Robots from Rhea[/h2]

[h3]The LightBot - Hermes-Class Lightweight Planetary Mapper[/h3]

[code][img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/43307026/553bf8276dab4733856b2e8c22fa336add15394b.png[/img]
                                           [i]The Hermes-Class LPM[/i][/code]
Originally designed for remote planetary exploration, the LPM, or "LightBot" as it's become known to the crew of Outpost Rhea is a small, highly maneuverable robot that makes use of several small hydrogen-based thrusters to remain airborne.

The Terra-Caelum Corporation had initially commissioned dozens of these bots for use in Outpost Rhea's experiments, although as the Station's focus shifted away from interplanetary exploration and more towards deep-space research, many of the units were shipped back Earthside and the few that remained were retrofitted to assist with menial labor and tight-space maintenance aboard the station.

The LPM's smaller frame and maneuverability allow it to traverse areas that the Human crew have difficulty reaching, such as crawlspaces, vents, and maintenance shafts.


[h3]The HeavyBot - Hephaestus-Class Heavyweight Industrial Loader[/h3]

[code][img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/43307026/e7abc8e76161fe0ddff089ec217dcb324dcb2672.png[/img]
                                           [i]The Hephaestus-Class HIL[/i][/code]
Built for use on heavy-duty construction sites, the Hephaestus HIL had assisted Terra-Caelum's many construction efforts in the Sol system, and when it came time for Outpost Rhea's construction, it just made sense to bring a handful out into deep-space with them.

Primarily tasked with hauling or towing overweight materials and machinery throughout the station, the HIL Units were also retrofitted to operate much of the station's infrastructure and technology to help make expansion of Rhea's frame more autonomous and less risky for their fleshy Human counterparts in the Engineering department. As the crew began to rely on the Hephaestus-class more and more, they earned the affectionate nickname "Hephty", or in some other cases, just "HeavyBot".

As part of this autonomy, and since the HIL Units were intended for use in hazardous environments, they are able to bypass many of the Station's quarantine shields, as well as access areas of the station where only high-level executives of TC Corp. are allowed.


Together, Players will take on the role of one of these bots and explore the calamity that left Outpost Rhea abandoned...


[h2]That's all for this week! [/h2]
I'll be back in another two weeks to cover what's next for our VA Cast, and hopefully give you all some names! But 'till then, take care of yourselves!

If you have read our [url=https://store.steampowered.com/news/app/2220420/view/3666529724079722183]last devlog,[/url] you'd know that we have officially made the decision to delay the game a little later into Q3 of this year, aiming ideally for the end of August. A number of factors have contributed to this; The team being forced to work out of home, our applications for further funding from Government Sources here in Australia, and the work that has stemmed from these processes have had an impact on the time we've been able to dedicate to the game, and here's why:

[h2]Working From Home[/h2]
Game development is a very collaborative medium - As such, working remotely impacts efficiency of communications and workflows, as well as leaves us more susceptible to software, hardware, and network issues. We're hoping to get good news soon and finally move into our office space, but until then, we're stuck working in this reduced capacity.

[h2]Funding Applications[/h2]
Since mid-December of 2022, we've been looking into external funding from two Government departments here in Australia, VicScreens (who are in charge of funding on a State level here in Victoria), and ScreenAustralia (the Federal counterpart that operates for Australia at large). These processes have seen us attending meetings, drafting new documentation, and filling in application forms for the better part of the past two months - The endgame for these applications is being able to pay the team a proper salary and allow us to leave our part-time work to focus on Regolith fully.
We've recently completed all our applications and are now just waiting on review processes - hopefully there will be more to share on this front in the coming month.

[h2]To Briefly Summarize[/h2]
Since the beginning of 2023 we've had a lot of extra stuff on our plate to handle outside of the game, and we're working through it as best we can - However, due to the amount of time we've lost as a result, we made the difficult decision to delay.
We hope you all understand, and we'll continue to keep you updated as important changes occur.

notes.title: Public Devlog #02 - Meeting the Team
notes.content:
Hello again, welcome back to another Dev Log!

A couple of weeks ago I outlined our current Alpha Milestone for the game, you can read all about it [url=https://store.steampowered.com/news/app/2220420/view/3682289786419344956]here[/url]. This week we thought you'd like to learn a little more about the team behind Regolith here.

The four of us met during our time as students at the Academy of Interactive Entertainment here in Melbourne, Australia. We've each worked together on a number of student and personal projects. Back in early 2022 we made a silly little comedy game for the Brackeys Game Jam, called [url=https://regolith-interactive.itch.io/as-seen-on-tv]As Seen On TV[/url].

The main dev team is made up of the four of us:

[h2]Conor Calam[/h2]
Hello again! I'm Conor, the programmer behind all the mechanics you see in Project Regolith - I'm also responsible for writing up our community updates, so you're all probably a little familiar with me at this stage! As for my background, I originally studied Game Design at AIE Melbourne, before moving on to Business Management and expanding my programming skills whilst working alongside the rest of the team here at Regolith! Since I was a kid I've always had a passion for coop games, and have a lot of strong memories of couch-coop with friends and family. I'm ecstatic to be working with such talented people and to have the support of an amazing community like you guys, and can't wait to show off more of Project Regolith to you all!

[h2]Harrison McNeil[/h2]
Harrison here! It's my job to design and implement the various puzzles/levels into Project Regolith, I studied Game Design and Production at AIE alongside both Conor and Ryan, it was in my second year of study when I first met Brandon who was doing the Art and Animation course at AIE.  After finishing my game design course I moved on to study Business Management alongside Conor and Brandon where we eventually founded Regolith Interactive. It wasn't long after where we looked to Ryan to be our Producer and officially join the team.  As far back as I can remember I've always loved video games, especially ones that I can play with friends and family, to be able to work on a co-op game with such like minded people people is an experience like no other.

[h2]Brandon Russell[/h2]
Hello! I'm Brandon, the Art Director for Project Regolith. I mainly create all the visuals that you see in-game. That includes 3D modelling of characters and the environment, textures, VFX, lighting and animations. I studied game art and animation for two years and business in games for an additional year, which led us to creating Project Regolith. I'm currently working in the games industry as a 3D artist, but try to balance working on the game outside of that!

[h2]Ryan Lovell[/h2]
I'm Ryan, the Producer and Lead Writer for Project Regolith. I'm the one responsible for writing every spoken and written word present in Project Regolith and also responsible for writing most of the paperwork here at the studio.  I have a previous background in filmmaking (Bachelor of Film Production SAE) mostly focused in screenwriting, direction and production management. So, after deciding to leave film for games and completing my education at AIE, my role here at Regolith is a natural fit for me. I'm the currently the only non-founding member of Regolith but this teams commitment to coop experiences is so in touch with my favorite experiences with video games, I'm proud of the work we're currently doing on Project Regolith and hope its the first of many great titles I'll get to help create.

Conor here again, and that's all for this week's update! See you all again in a couple of weeks for a progress update! If you haven't already, don't forget to join the [url=https://discord.gg/EpwKaVbJfk]Discord[/url] and [url=https://twitter.com/Regolith_Int]follow[/url] [url=https://www.instagram.com/regolith_interactive/]all[/url] [url=https://www.tiktok.com/@regolith_interactive]our[/url] [url=https://www.linkedin.com/company/89682847]Socials[/url]!

See you soon,

- Conor
